---
title: Parameters over time
jupyter: python3
---

So far, every rate in the measles model has been the same from the first day to the last. Over the course of years, that is rarely true. Before vaccination, measles came in large epidemics every year or two, peaking at the same time each year, and studies of these epidemics in England and Wales found that their timing followed the school calendar: transmission among children rose when schools opened and fell in the holidays. Birth rates change over decades too, and with them the number of new susceptible children.

This tutorial makes the parameters of the model change over time, in three ways: a smooth yearly cycle, a school calendar, and a trend over years. Then it gives a value that differs by age group and in time at once.

By the end of this tutorial, you will be able to:

- give a parameter a yearly cycle with `ss.seasonal()`;
- give a parameter values on dates, repeating each year or not, with `ss.timeseries()`;
- give a parameter a value for each group that also changes in time, with `ss.by()`;
- explain how seasonal transmission and births shape the pattern of measles epidemics.

## The model so far

This is the SEIR model of measles from [Tutorial 3](t3_structure.qmd), run for 30 years with births and deaths, as in [Tutorial 4](t4_ages.qmd). For now it has no age groups. Since each section below gives β in a different way, the disease is made by a function of β.

A few things differ from the shorter runs of earlier tutorials:

- **The rates have units.** The birth rate is per year and β per day, so β is given as `ss.perday(1.9)` rather than as a bare number, so that each says its own unit.
- **The results are weekly.** `dt=ss.weeks(1)` records the results once a week, which is plenty over 30 years; as an ODE, the model is still solved finely in between.
- **The town starts near its long-run balance.** After decades of measles, most people in a town are immune, and only about 1 in R0 (here 1 in 15, about 7%) are susceptible: just enough for each infection to cause one more, on average. `init` gives the share of people in each state at the start, and the rest start in `R` (the run notes this).
- **Births and deaths** are 30 a year per 1,000 people, a birth rate typical of England and Wales in the early 20th century, or of many countries today.

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True) # Plots and tables suited to a notebook

def make_measles(beta):
    """ The SEIR model of measles, with the transmission rate β given """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    infection   = S >> E @ beta*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10) # Latent for 10 days on average
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)  # Infectious for 8 days on average
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(S=0.07, E=0.0003, I=0.0003))
    return measles

demographics = [ss.birth(rate=ss.peryear(0.03)), ss.death(rate=ss.peryear(0.03))] # 30 a year per 1,000 people
pars = dict(demographics=demographics, total_pop=100_000, start='2000-01-01', stop='2030-01-01', dt=ss.weeks(1))

measles = make_measles(ss.perday(1.9))
sim = ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.plot()
```

(As in [Tutorial 2](t2_model.qmd), the R0 that the run prints is the reproduction number at the start, about 1 here, since 93% of people are immune; R0 itself is 15.)

The epidemics are large at first, then smaller, and within about 20 years the number of infectious people settles at a steady level, at which new infections just balance the births of new susceptible children. This is what an SEIR model with births does when its rates are constant, but not what measles did: its epidemics kept coming. What kept them going was a rate that changed over the year.

## A yearly cycle

`ss.seasonal()` gives a value that rises and falls once a year: `mean × (1 + amplitude × cos(2π(t − peak)))`, with `t` in years. Here β is 1.9 per day on average, 20% higher than that at its peak in January, and 20% lower in July:

```{python}
beta = ss.seasonal(mean=ss.perday(1.9), amplitude=0.2, peak='January')
measles = make_measles(beta)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.plot()
```

Now the epidemics don't die down: after a few years, a large epidemic comes every second year, peaking in the spring, with a much smaller one in the years between. A large epidemic uses up so many susceptible people that, by the next season of high transmission, births have not yet replaced enough of them for another; by the one after, they have. A cycle in β of only 20% either way is enough to keep this going indefinitely, and the two-year rhythm comes from the model itself: from R0, the latent and infectious periods, and the birth rate, not from anything that happens every two years.

## A school calendar

A smooth cycle is a convenient approximation. The seasonality of measles is thought to come mostly from school terms, which start and stop on dates. `ss.timeseries()` gives a value at each of a set of times: here, how much transmission changes in each part of the school year, 20% higher than β in term and half of it in the holidays (a simplified calendar, with holidays at Christmas and in the summer). Between the dates, a value holds until the next one (`mode='constant'`, the default; `'linear'` would change it gradually). `period=ss.years(1)` repeats the calendar of the year 2000 every year:

```{python}
school = ss.timeseries({
    '2000-01-01': 0.5, # New Year holidays
    '2000-01-07': 1.2, # Spring and summer terms
    '2000-07-20': 0.5, # Summer holidays
    '2000-09-03': 1.2, # Autumn term
    '2000-12-20': 0.5, # Christmas holidays
}, period=ss.years(1))

measles = make_measles(ss.perday(1.9)*school)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, **pars)
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.plot()
```

The holidays are 63 days of the year, so on average over the year, β is about 8% higher than 1.9 a day. Again there is a large epidemic every second year, but now each one grows through the spring and summer terms and stops abruptly when the summer holidays begin, and smaller ones come in the autumn term between them. This two-year cycle, with epidemics that end with the school year, is what measles did in large cities in England and Wales from the 1950s until vaccination began, and models with term-time forcing like this one were among the first to explain it.

A time series can hold any value that changes in time, not only a factor: a rate (`ss.timeseries({'2000-01-01': ss.perday(1.9), ...})`), a duration, or the coverage of an intervention. It can also be read from a file with a column of dates and a column of values (`ss.timeseries('school_terms.csv')`).

## A trend over years

Without `period=`, a time series doesn't repeat: before its first time it has its first value, and after its last time, its last. With `mode='linear'`, it changes steadily between them. Here the birth and death rates both fall by half over the 30 years, from 30 to 15 per 1,000 people a year, as they did in many countries over the 20th century. Since they are equal, the population stays the same size:

```{python}
birth_rate = ss.timeseries({'2000-01-01': ss.peryear(0.03), '2030-01-01': ss.peryear(0.015)}, mode='linear')
demographics = [ss.birth(rate=birth_rate), ss.death(rate=birth_rate)] # Equal, so the population stays the same size

measles = make_measles(ss.perday(1.9)*school)
sim = ss.Sim(measles, **(pars | dict(demographics=demographics)))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.plot()
```

(`pars | dict(...)` is the same parameters as before, with `demographics` replaced.) As fewer children are born, fewer susceptible people are added each year, so the epidemics get smaller, and the clear two-year rhythm of the first decade gives way to smaller epidemics every year, of uneven size. The same model, with only the birth rate changed, gives a different pattern of epidemics: one reason why measles behaved so differently in different places and decades, even before vaccination.

## Values by group, and in time

In the model so far, the school calendar changes transmission for everyone. In reality it changes the contacts of children. With age groups and a contact matrix, as in [Tutorial 4](t4_ages.qmd), `ss.by()` gives a value for each age group, and each value can itself change in time. Here children's transmission follows the school calendar, and adults' doesn't:

```{python}
def make_measles_by_age():
    """ The SEIR model of measles, by age, with school terms for children """
    S, E, I, R = ss.states('S E I R')
    beta = ss.perday(0.14) # Per contact
    in_school = ss.by(age=[school, 1, 1]) # The school calendar for ages 0-14; no change for 15-64 or 65+
    infection   = S >> E @ beta*in_school*I
    progression = E >> I @ ss.days(10)
    recovery    = I >> R @ ss.days(8)
    measles = ss.Disease(infection, progression, recovery, init=dict(S=0.07, E=0.0003, I=0.0003))
    measles.stratify(age={0: 0.3, 15: 0.6, 65: 0.1})
    return measles

contacts = ss.contacts(ages=[0, 15, 65], matrix=[[10, 4, 1], [4, 8, 2], [1, 2, 3]])
measles = make_measles_by_age()
sim = ss.Sim(measles, networks=contacts, **(pars | dict(stop='2020-01-01')))
sim.run()
sim.results.measles.I.by('age').plot()
```

The run is for 20 years, and people now move up the age groups as they get older, since they are born and die. A value by group multiplies the rate of infection of the people in that group, so here it is children's chance of infection per contact that rises in term. (This is a simplification: closing schools mainly reduces children's contacts with each other, not their contacts with adults.) Most infections are in children, as before vaccination, and the epidemics follow the school year.

::: {.callout-warning}
## [PROPOSAL]
Two spellings of the same value fail. `ss.perday(0.14) * ss.by(age=[school, 1, 1])`, assigned to a variable before it is used in a rate, raises `IncompatibleTypes` ("a rate (ss.perday) * timeseries has no meaning"), though the same product written inside the rate (`beta*in_school*I`, as above) works. And `ss.by(age=[ss.perday(0.14)*school, ss.perday(0.14), ss.perday(0.14)])` is accepted, but the run fails with `TypeError: float() argument must be a string or a real number, not 'BinOp'`. A value by group that is a number times a time series should work wherever it is written (P11).
:::

## Fitting a value that changes in time

Any of these values can be fitted to data, by giving the part to fit as an `ss.par()` with bounds ([Tutorial 7](t7_calibration.qmd)). For example, the average of a seasonal β, with the amplitude fixed:

```python
beta = ss.seasonal(mean=ss.par(ss.perday(1.9), bounds=[ss.perday(1), ss.perday(3)], name='beta'), amplitude=0.2, peak='January')
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## [PROPOSAL]
Without `name='beta'`, the model can't be built: "Could not find a name for the parameter 1.9 used in "infection"; give it one, e.g. ss.par(1.9, name="infection_p")". A parameter in the mean of a seasonal value should be named from where it is used, as a number written in a rate is (`beta`), so that `name=` is needed only to choose another name (P13). The parameters then include both `beta` and `beta_infection` (the seasonal value as a whole), which is confusing; only the parameter to fit should be listed by its own name.
:::

Every solver follows a value that changes in time within each step (the Gillespie solver approximately, with a note), so these values work the same way as compartments or as agents. For more on the forms a parameter can take, see [Parameters](../user_guide/models_parameters.qmd).

## Exercises

1. In the model with the seasonal β, move the peak of transmission from January to July. Do the epidemics now peak in a different month? By how much does the timing of the peak of infections lag behind the peak of transmission?
2. In the model with the school calendar, raise the birth and death rates to 45 a year per 1,000 people. What happens to the two-year cycle? (Higher birth rates were one reason measles was yearly, not every two years, in some places.)
3. The ODE follows the expected numbers, which never reach zero, but in a town of 100,000 people, the number infectious in the troughs between epidemics is small. Run the model with the school calendar as a stochastic model, `sim.run(solver='binomial')`, with several random seeds (`ss.Sim(..., rand_seed=1)`, and so on). Does measles persist for the 30 years? Since nothing brings it back into the town once it is gone, what does this suggest about the size of population that measles needs in order to persist?
